topics.definition: Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) is, in IMO's words, a structured and systematic methodology aimed at enhancing maritime safety, including protection of life, health, the marine environment and property, by using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment (MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, para 1.1.1). It is a tool for the IMO rule-making process: a Member State or an organisation in consultative status uses it to support a proposal for new or amended rules, or a Committee uses it to evaluate one. It runs in five steps — identification of hazards, risk analysis, risk control options, cost-benefit assessment and recommendations for decision-making — and it recommends; the MSC or MEPC decides. Human Reliability Analysis (HRA), set out in Appendix 1 of the same guidelines, is the accepted way of bringing the human contribution to system failure into an FSA, using task analysis, human error identification and, where needed, quantification techniques such as THERP and HEART. The Human Element Analysing Process (HEAP) is IMO's companion flowchart for making sure the human element is considered whenever rules are developed.
why: Examiners test the boundary. The commonest error is to describe FSA as 'the risk assessment we do on board'. FSA is IMO's rule-making methodology; the shipboard and company risk assessment is ISM Code 1.2.2.2. A Chief Engineer who keeps the two apart answers the follow-up questions with confidence.

The rules a C/E works under were shaped by FSA. Knowing that a requirement went through hazard identification, risk analysis and a cost-effectiveness test explains why IMO adopts some measures and not others.

The vocabulary carries over. Risk as frequency × consequence, the risk matrix, ALARP and 'cost per unit of risk reduction' are the same ideas a C/E uses when defending a maintenance or retrofit proposal to the office.

The human element is examined from both sides. HRA and HEAP show how IMO tries to design rules that people can actually follow — the link between this topic and the Human Element material in Part 27 · Topic 2.
Wording matters in the written paper. Step names, GCAF/NCAF and 'recommendations, not decisions' are easy marks when stated in IMO wording, and easy to lose when they are not.

sections.head: 🏛️ What FSA Is — and What It Is Not

body.p: The source opens with IMO's own definition, and it is accurate: FSA is a structured and systematic methodology aimed at enhancing maritime safety — protection of life, health, the marine environment and property — by using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment. The source's gloss 'taking action before disaster occurs' is also right: the guidelines describe the proactive nature of FSA as one of its most beneficial qualities, because hazard identification is not confined to hazards that have already caused accidents.

body.p: This boundary is the first thing to state in an oral answer. A Chief Engineer does not 'carry out an FSA' before overhauling a purifier; he carries out a risk assessment under the SMS. An earlier summary of the five steps is at Simon Notes Part 6 · Note 1 (FSA); this topic teaches the current Rev.2 position in full.

sections.head: 🪜 The Five Steps in IMO Wording

body.p: FSA starts from a problem definition (the ship category, systems, operations and external influences under study), which is not one of the numbered steps. The five steps then follow, and step 5 interacts with each of the others (MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, para 3.1.1.1).

head: Step (IMO wording)
What it does
What the source wrote
rows: 1 — Identification of hazards

Produces a list of hazards and associated scenarios, prioritised by risk level. Uses creative and analytical techniques in structured group reviews (HAZID) with experts in design, operation and management; scenarios are ranked on a risk matrix of frequency and consequence. What is studied depends on the ship type, cargo and operation — the source's 'ship type, cargo, trading pattern'
'Identification of Hazards' — correct
2 — Risk analysis

Investigates in detail the causes, initiating events and consequences of the more important scenarios from step 1, using risk models such as fault trees and event trees, and identifies the high-risk areas (accident scenarios) for the ship type or problem under review
'Assesment of Risks' (PDF 675) / 'Risk Analysis' (PDF 676); 'high risk areas of ship'
3 — Risk control options

Identifies risk control measures (RCMs) for the high-risk areas and groups them into a limited number of risk control options (RCOs) usable as practical regulatory options. Four stages: focus on the risk areas needing control; identify potential RCMs; evaluate each RCM's effectiveness by re-running the step 2 analysis (including side-effects and interdependencies); group RCMs into practical options
'decide which hazard can be avoided' — step 3 does not decide
4 — Cost-benefit assessment
Identifies and compares the costs and benefits of each RCO over its life and ranks the RCOs by cost-effectiveness — cost per unit of risk reduction (GCAF/NCAF)
'Cost Benefit Assesment' / 'Cost Benefit Analysis'; 'cost must be lesser than the damage'
5 — Recommendations for decision-making

Defines recommendations for the decision-makers, presented in an auditable and traceable manner, based on: ranking of hazards and their underlying causes; ranking of RCOs by costs and benefits; and identification of the RCOs that keep risk as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
'a final decision taken' — FSA recommends, MSC/MEPC decide

sections.head: 📐 Risk, the Risk Index and ALARP

body.p: The guidelines define risk as the combination of the frequency and the severity of the consequence. For ranking scenarios at the end of step 1, Appendix 4 recommends logarithmic frequency and severity indices, so that risk = probability × consequence becomes log(risk) = log(probability) + log(consequence). The Risk Index is therefore the sum of the two indices: RI = FI + SI. The guidelines' own example: an event rated 'remote' (FI = 3) with severity 'significant' (SI = 2) gives RI = 5.

head: Region (Appendix 5)
Meaning
Action
rows: Intolerable
Above the upper bound
Risk cannot be justified and must be reduced irrespective of cost
ALARP region
Between the bounds — neither negligibly low nor intolerably high
Reduce risk unless the cost is disproportionate to the benefit; 'reasonable' is interpreted as cost-effective, examined by a cost-effectiveness analysis
Broadly acceptable (negligible)
Below the lower bound
No further risk reduction required

ul: ALARP — As Low As Reasonably Practicable. The guidelines record that, according to several researchers, most risks in shipping fall in the ALARP region (not yet verified for all ship types), so most risk-based decisions need a cost-effectiveness analysis.
FN curve — a plot of the cumulative frequency (F) of accidents with N or more fatalities against N; it represents societal risk (risk to a whole group of people), alongside individual risk.
The risk matrix used for initial ranking is a ranking tool, not a pass/fail test: the real test of a risk control option comes in steps 3 and 4.

sections.head: 💲 Step 4 — Cost-Effectiveness Indices (PDF 691)

body.p: The source correctly places these indices in step 4. The guidelines say there are several indices which express cost-effectiveness in relation to safety of life, and name two: GCAF and NCAF (para 8.2.2; Appendix 7).

head: Index
Definition (Appendix 7)
Reading it
rows: GCAF — Gross Cost of Averting a Fatality
Marginal (additional) cost of the RCO ÷ reduction in risk to personnel, in fatalities averted: GCAF = ΔC / ΔR
Considered first; a pure cost-per-life test
NCAF — Net Cost of Averting a Fatality
(Marginal cost of the RCO − economic benefit of the RCO) ÷ fatalities averted: NCAF = (ΔC − ΔB) / ΔR
Credits the money the RCO saves (e.g. avoided damage); a negative NCAF means the monetary benefits exceed the costs

body.p: Each RCO's GCAF/NCAF is compared with a cost-effectiveness criterion. Appendix 7 gives US$3 million per fatality averted (a criterion covering fatalities, injuries and ill health) as an illustrative value, derived from societal indicators and to be updated regularly; the value actually used in a study must be stated explicitly. GCAF is considered first; NCAF may also be considered when an RCO is close to the criterion. An RCO whose cost per fatality averted is within the criterion is regarded as cost-effective. That replaces the source's rule of thumb 'cost of solution must be less than the damage'.

head: Term listed in the source
What it actually is (Appendix 7)
rows: DALY — Disability Adjusted Life Years
A measure of health loss (with QALY, Quality Adjusted Life Years) used to express injuries and ill health — not a cost-effectiveness index
LQI — Life Quality Index
A societal indicator of quality of life; one of the bases from which the GCAF/NCAF criterion values are derived — not itself a cost-effectiveness index

body.p: Worked illustration (numbers invented for teaching): an RCO costs US$40 million across the fleet over its life and is estimated to avert 20 fatalities. GCAF = 40 ÷ 20 = US$2 million per fatality averted — below the illustrative US$3 million criterion, so it is cost-effective. If it also avoids US$10 million of damage, NCAF = (40 − 10) ÷ 20 = US$1.5 million.

sections.head: 🧭 HEAP — the Human Element Analysing Process (PDF 690)

body.p: HEAP is IMO's Human Element Analysing Process — not the 'Human Element Analysis Program' of the source. MSC/Circ.878–MEPC/Circ.346 (20 November 1998) describes it as a practical tool, a flowchart listing a series of questions that should be considered so that the human element is properly addressed in the regulatory development process. It answers the Assembly's human element goal (A.850(20), as cited in the circular) of having a structured approach to human element issues in the development of regulations and guidelines by all Committees and Sub-Committees.

ul: When it is used: while IMO instruments are being introduced or amended — not 'whenever a new amendment enters into force', as the source says. By entry into force the rule is already made.
What it looks at: the ship and its equipment, the master and crew, and the wider work environment that a proposed rule will affect.
Who uses it: regulators — IMO Committees, Sub-Committees and Member Governments.
Link with FSA: MSC/Circ.1022–MEPC/Circ.391 (2002) gives guidance on using HEAP and FSA together in the IMO rule-making process.
Not the same as the checklist: MSC-MEPC.7/Circ.1 (22 May 2006) is the separate Checklist for considering human element issues by IMO bodies. Do not cite it as the HEAP document.

sections.head: 🧠 Human Reliability Analysis — Appendix 1 of the FSA Guidelines (PDF 692)

body.p: HRA is a process — a set of activities that may use a number of techniques — for assessing the contribution of the human element to system failure. It may be qualitative or quantitative depending on the level of FSA being undertaken. IMO's FSA Guidelines carry HRA guidance as Appendix 1, describing it as the accepted way of incorporating the human element into quantitative risk assessment and FSA.

Where HRA came from. HRA was developed primarily for the nuclear industry and IMO says it must be adapted for ships: a nuclear plant has many automatic protection systems, so the human element can be considered after the system performance, whereas on board the human has a greater freedom to disrupt the system, so a high-level task analysis is needed at the outset of an FSA. The techniques below (THERP, HEART, task analysis) were born in nuclear and process safety and are adopted within FSA — they are not IMO inventions.

The usual HRA stages (App.1 para 1.1.3) are: (1) identification of key tasks; (2) task analysis of key tasks; (3) human error identification; (4) human error analysis; (5) human reliability quantification. Appendix 1 then fits HRA into the FSA steps as follows.

head: FSA step
HRA contribution (Appendix 1)
rows: 1 — Identification of hazards
Identify the key human tasks and interactions which, if not performed correctly, could lead to system failure — a broad scoping exercise, with a high-level task analysis strongly advised
2 — Risk analysis
Detailed task analysis, human error analysis and, where a quantified FSA is needed, human error quantification
3 — Risk control options

Human-element measures are treated like other risk control measures — to reduce the frequency of failure, mitigate its effects, alleviate the circumstances in which failures occur, or mitigate the consequences of accidents
4 — Cost-benefit assessment
No specific HRA guidance
5 — Recommendations
HRA results contribute to balanced decisions and recommendations of the whole FSA

ul: Human error probability (HEP) = number of human errors that have occurred ÷ number of opportunities for human error.
Performance shaping factors can help or hinder performance; error producing conditions are those with a negative effect.

Experienced practitioners get the greatest benefit from the early, qualitative stages — task analysis and error identification. Maritime human error data are limited, so expert judgement is often needed for quantification and must be justified.

sections.head: 🔢 Quantification Methods — THERP and HEART

body.p: The guidelines name THERP and HEART as the two main HRA methods that come with databases of human error probabilities (mainly from the nuclear industry). They are not the only HRA methods: expert judgement techniques such as absolute probability judgement are also described.

head: THERP — Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction
HEART — Human Error Assessment and Reduction Technique
rows: Origin
Swain and Guttmann (1983), Sandia National Laboratories, for the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NUREG/CR-1278)
J.C. Williams (1985)
Nature
Both a human reliability technique and a human error databank; described by IMO as the most widely used human error quantitative prediction technique
Considers the ergonomic, task and environmental factors that adversely affect performance
How it models
Probability trees and models of dependence, plus performance shaping factors (PSFs) affecting action
Quantifies how far each factor independently affects performance; the HEP is a function of the product of the factors identified for the task
Strength
Particularly effective in quantifying errors in highly procedural activities
Gives specific information on remedial measures to combat human error
Limitation
Critically dependent on its database of human error probabilities
Generic data mainly derived from the nuclear industry; needs adaptation for ships

sections.head: 📋 Task Analysis — High-level, Detailed and Extended (PDF 693–694)

body.p: Task analysis is a collection of techniques that compare the demands of a system with the capabilities of the operator, usually to improve performance by reducing errors. IMO's HRA guidance summarises three types (Appendix 1, Table 2). There are many more task-analysis techniques; the most widely used is Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA), developed by Annett and Duncan (1967).

head: Type
What it identifies
rows: High-level task analysis
A broad but shallow overview: the main functions to be performed to achieve an operational goal — normal, emergency, maintenance and recovery — recorded hierarchically or in a table
Detailed task analysis

Six elements: (1) the overall task; (2) the sub-tasks; (3) the people who contribute to each task and their interactions; (4) how the work is done — working practices in normal and emergency situations; (5) the controls, displays and tools used; (6) the factors influencing performance
Extended task analysis (XTA)
Used where the focus is less on what action is performed and more on the reasons for the decisions taken — a cognitive approach suited to decision-making tasks such as navigation decisions

body.p: XTA activities (Johnson and Johnson, 1987, as summarised by IMO): (1) interview on the conditions that enable or disable actions and how changes affect choices; (2) qualitative analysis of the recorded, transcribed data (for example Grounded Theory); (3) representation of the analysis in an appropriate format — systemic grammar networks; (4) validation activities, such as observation and testing hypotheses.

Illustrative shipboard example: for changing over a main engine from heavy fuel to distillate, a detailed task analysis lists the sub-tasks, who does each one and which valves, gauges and alarms are used; an XTA asks why the engineer chose the change-over rate he did — the knowledge, cues and pressures behind the decision.

qa: What is Formal Safety Assessment, and who uses it?

FSA is defined by IMO as a structured and systematic methodology aimed at enhancing maritime safety, including protection of life, health, the marine environment and property, by using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment. It is a tool for the IMO rule-making process: a Member State or an organisation in consultative status uses it to support a proposal for new or amended rules, and a Committee can use it to evaluate a proposal. The current guidelines are MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2 of 9 April 2018. It is proactive — it looks for hazards before they cause accidents. It is not the shipboard or company risk assessment required by ISM Code 1.2.2.2; on board we assess the risks of our own tasks under the SMS.
Name the five steps of FSA and what each produces.

After a problem definition, step 1 is identification of hazards, which produces a list of hazards and scenarios ranked by risk using HAZID sessions and a risk matrix. Step 2 is risk analysis, which models the causes and consequences of the most important scenarios with tools such as fault and event trees and identifies the high-risk areas. Step 3 is risk control options: risk control measures are identified, their effect is tested by re-running the risk analysis, and they are grouped into practical options. Step 4 is cost-benefit assessment, which compares the costs and benefits of each option and ranks them by cost-effectiveness. Step 5 is recommendations for decision-making, presented to the MSC or MEPC in an auditable and traceable way. Step 5 interacts with all the others.
What are GCAF and NCAF, and how are they used?

They are the cost-effectiveness indices for safety of life in FSA step 4. GCAF, the Gross Cost of Averting a Fatality, is the marginal cost of a risk control option divided by the reduction in fatalities it achieves. NCAF, the Net Cost of Averting a Fatality, first subtracts the economic benefit of the option, such as avoided damage; a negative NCAF means the option pays for itself. GCAF is considered first. Each value is compared with a criterion; Appendix 7 of the guidelines gives US$3 million per fatality averted as an illustrative figure. DALY and LQI are related terms in the same appendix — DALY measures health loss and the LQI is used to derive the criterion — but they are not themselves cost-effectiveness indices.
What is ALARP, and how does it fit into FSA?

ALARP means as low as reasonably practicable. The guidelines divide risk into three regions: intolerable, where risk must be reduced whatever the cost; broadly acceptable, where no further reduction is needed; and the ALARP region in between, where risk should be reduced unless the cost is disproportionate to the benefit. 'Reasonable' is interpreted as cost-effective, so in the ALARP region the decision is made by the cost-effectiveness analysis in step 4. Step 5 then recommends the options that keep risk ALARP. The guidelines note that most shipping risks are thought to lie in this region.
What is Human Reliability Analysis, and what are THERP and HEART?

HRA is a process for assessing the human contribution to system failure. It was developed primarily for the nuclear industry, and IMO adopted it as Appendix 1 of the FSA Guidelines as the accepted way to bring the human element into FSA. Its usual stages are identification of key tasks, task analysis, human error identification, human error analysis and, where needed, human reliability quantification; the qualitative stages give most of the benefit. THERP, the Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction by Swain and Guttmann in 1983, uses probability trees, dependence models and performance shaping factors and is most effective for highly procedural tasks, but depends on its error database. HEART, the Human Error Assessment and Reduction Technique by Williams, multiplies the effects of error-producing conditions and points directly to remedial measures.
What is HEAP, and how does it differ from the IMO human element checklist?

HEAP is the Human Element Analysing Process, issued as interim guidelines in MSC/Circ.878–MEPC/Circ.346 in 1998. It is a flowchart of questions that helps regulators make sure all human element aspects — the ship and equipment, the master and crew, the work environment — are considered while an IMO instrument is being developed or amended. MSC/Circ.1022–MEPC/Circ.391 of 2002 gives guidance on using HEAP with FSA. The checklist in MSC-MEPC.7/Circ.1 of 2006 is a separate document that IMO bodies complete when considering human element issues in amendments. deep_dive.title: Case Study — How an FSA on Engine-Room Fires Would Be Built (illustrative)
blocks: A Member State is concerned about engine-room fires from fuel leaks on to hot surfaces in a class of cargo ship and decides to submit an FSA to the MSC supporting an amendment. The ship type, the hazard category and the scope are written up as the problem definition. No real IMO submission is described here; the figures are invented for teaching.

A HAZID panel of designers, operators, a class surveyor and serving engineers lists scenarios — a fuel pipe fracture spraying on to an exhaust manifold, a filter cover left loose after cleaning, a leak during bunkering. Each is given a frequency index and severity index, and the risk index ranks them. Step 2 builds a fault tree for 'fuel ignites on hot surface' and an event tree for what follows — detection, shutdown, local suppression, evacuation. The HRA module identifies the key human task (filter cleaning and re-assembly), analyses it in detail and uses a quantification technique for the probability of leaving the cover loose under time pressure.

Risk control measures are listed — better insulation of hot surfaces, screening of pressure pipe joints, a design that prevents the cover being refitted wrongly, better leak detection. Grouped into options, each is re-run through the step 2 model. Step 4 costs each option over the ship's life: one option costs US$40 million across the fleet and averts an estimated 20 fatalities, a GCAF of US$2 million — inside the illustrative US$3 million criterion. Step 5 recommends that option to the MSC in a traceable report. HEAP questions are asked along the way: can a crew of this size actually carry out the new checks?

FSA is a regulator's study of a ship type, built from hazard identification, risk models, human reliability and cost-effectiveness, ending in a recommendation. The Chief Engineer meets its results as rules. On his own ship he uses the same logic — hazards, risks, controls, cost — in an ISM risk assessment, and he should never call that an FSA.

topics.definition: Root cause analysis (RCA) is a structured way of finding the underlying causes of a problem, incident or non-conformity so that corrective action removes them and the problem does not recur, instead of only treating the immediate trigger. The source teaches five commonly used quality tools — the fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, Pareto analysis, the 5 Why technique, failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) and fault tree analysis (FTA) — then the difference between a proximate and a root cause, and James Reason's Swiss cheese model of accident causation, with its active failures and latent conditions. FMEA and FTA are also risk-analysis techniques used before anything goes wrong. On board, RCA is how ISM Code element 9 is made to work; in a casualty investigation, IMO leaves the choice of method to the investigator.
why: ISM 9.2 demands it. Corrective action must include measures intended to prevent recurrence — and recurrence is prevented only by fixing causes, not symptoms. Examiners expect a C/E to show how he closes a non-conformity properly.
Senthil asks for the tools by name. 'What RCA techniques do you know? Draw a fishbone. What is RPN?' are standard prompts, and a sketch on paper earns marks.
Repeated engine-room defects are a Pareto problem. A C/E with limited people and spares must find the few causes behind most of the downtime and act on those first.
Human error is rarely the root cause. The Swiss cheese model is the standard answer to '80% of accidents are caused by human error' — the question printed in the source's own exam insert.
Terms are easily confused. Investigation 'proximate cause' is not insurance 'causa proxima'; FMEA is not RCA proper; a contributing factor is not a root cause.

sections.head: 🔍 Why RCA — and Where IMO Stands

body.p: The source opens with the business case: no organisation is free of problems, and success depends on finding the root causes and acting on them. Done properly, RCA prevents recurrence, improves processes and raises overall performance. This is general quality-management practice; at sea it has a regulatory hook in ISM Code element 9, which requires non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences to be reported and analysed and corrective action taken, including measures intended to prevent recurrence.

ul: No RCA tool is IMO-prescribed. Resolution A.1075(28), the guidance for implementing the Casualty Investigation Code (MSC.255(84)), says analysis methods should be seen as 'tools in a tool box'; a good investigation chooses the set that suits the casualty.

What IMO does require is a systemic perspective — going beyond 'who did what?' to the conditions that influenced events, even when they lie far from the casualty site — and, as a minimum, a reconstruction of the sequence of events, the linked events and contributing factors at all appropriate levels, and a safety analysis with recommendations.
The five tools in the source are therefore good practice, not regulation. Say 'the company's SMS procedure uses 5 Why and a fishbone', not 'IMO requires 5 Why'.

sections.head: 🧩 Proximate Cause, Root Cause and Contributing Factor (PDF 684)

body.p: The source's two-column table is a good start. NASA's mishap-investigation definitions (NPR 8621.1D) give a fuller, recognised set of terms, and they correct the source's second line on root cause.

head: Term
Meaning
Test
rows: Proximate (direct) cause
The event or condition that existed immediately before the undesired outcome and directly resulted in it
If it had been eliminated, the outcome would have been prevented — 'for the moment', as the source rightly says, because the deeper causes remain
Intermediate cause
An event or condition between the root cause and the proximate cause
Links the organisational cause to the immediate failure
Root cause
An underlying event or condition, often organisational, that set off the chain; typically several root causes contribute
If eliminated or modified, it would have prevented the causal chain and the undesired outcome
Contributing factor
An event or condition that may have contributed to the outcome
Its removal alone would not have prevented the outcome — this is what the source's 'may or may not result in the event' actually describes

body.p: Do not confuse with insurance. In marine insurance, causa proxima is the dominant, effective cause of a loss for which the underwriter is liable — not necessarily the cause nearest in time (Part 17 · Topic 2). In an investigation, 'proximate cause' means the immediate cause, and the aim is to dig beneath it to the root causes.

sections.head: 🐟 Fishbone (Ishikawa / Cause-and-Effect) Diagram (PDF 679)

body.p: The fishbone diagram is also called the Ishikawa diagram (after Kaoru Ishikawa) or the cause-and-effect diagram. The problem or effect is written at the head; the spine leads to it; each main bone is a category of cause; smaller arrows on each bone are the primary causes, and arrows on those are secondary and tertiary (sub-)causes.

body.ascii:
MAN              MACHINE
   \  cause         \  cause ← subcause
    \  cause         \  cause
     \________________\________________→  PROBLEM / EFFECT
     /                /
    /  cause         /  cause
   /  cause         /  cause
MATERIAL          METHOD

ul: The source uses the classic 4M set — Man, Machine, Material, Method. A common 6M set adds Measurement and Mother Nature (environment). The categories are a prompt and can be changed to suit the problem (for example People, Procedures, Plant, Environment, Management).
Strength: it makes a team look across all categories instead of stopping at the first plausible cause.
Limitation: it lists possible causes; it does not prove which ones acted. Evidence, 5 Why or an FTA is needed to confirm them.

sections.head: 📊 Pareto Analysis (PDF 680)

body.p: Pareto analysis is known as the 80/20 rule: roughly 80% of the effects come from about 20% of the causes. The principle was named by J.M. Juran after the economist Vilfredo Pareto — the 'vital few and the trivial many'. The 80/20 split is a heuristic, not a law; real data may give 70/30 or 90/10. Its use is to identify and prioritise the few causes that contribute most to a problem.

ul: Construction: bars for each cause in descending order of frequency or impact (left axis), with a cumulative-percentage line on a 0–100% right-hand axis (10% steps, including 90%). The causes to the left of where the line flattens are the vital few.
Choose the measure carefully: counting occurrences can rank a hundred nuisance alarms above one main-engine stoppage; weighting by downtime hours or cost gives a truer picture.

Illustrative shipboard use: a year of unplanned stoppages sorted by cause shows that fuel-system faults and purifier upsets account for most lost hours, so the C/E's corrective-action plan starts there.

body.p: Pareto is a prioritisation tool rather than a root-cause tool: it tells you where to dig, and fishbone, 5 Why or FTA then find the causes.

sections.head: ❓ The 5 Why Technique (PDF 681)

body.p: Asking 'why?' repeatedly uncovers the underlying causes of a problem; asking about five times aims to get past the symptoms to a root cause. The technique comes from the Toyota Production System, described by Taiichi Ohno, and is commonly credited to Sakichi Toyoda. 'Five' is a rule of thumb — stop when the answer is a cause the organisation can act on.

head: Why?
Answer (illustrative example)
rows: Why did the generator trip?
Low fuel pressure at the engine
Why was the fuel pressure low?
The duplex filter was choked
Why was it choked?
It had not been changed over and cleaned at the scheduled interval
Why was it missed?
The task was not in the planned maintenance system after the filter was replaced with a new model
Why was it not in the PMS?
The equipment change procedure did not require the PMS to be updated — the root cause, and the corrective action

body.p: Limitation: 5 Why follows a single chain and depends on the investigator. Casualties usually have several interacting causes, so for anything serious combine it with a fishbone, an FTA or a systemic method, as A.1075(28) expects.

sections.head: ⚙️ FMEA — a Proactive Risk-Analysis Technique (PDF 682)

body.p: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) is a systematic, structured approach that identifies the potential failure modes of a system or component, with their causes and effects, so that they can be prevented or mitigated before they occur, and prioritises the actions. That makes it a proactive (prospective) risk-analysis technique, not root cause analysis of an event that has already happened; it complements reactive RCA. IMO lists FMEA among the hazard identification and risk analysis techniques for FSA (Topic 1). Its extended form with a criticality assessment is FMECA.

head: Step
What is done
Source wording
rows: Define the system; identify potential failure modes (team brainstorming)
'Identify Failure Modes through Brain Storming'
Identify the effects of each failure mode; rate Severity (S), 1–10
'Severerity Assesment'
Identify the causes; rate Occurrence (O), 1–10
'Probability number of occurance'
Identify current controls; rate Detection (D) — how well they detect the cause or failure mode, 1–10
'Evaluate the effect of Detection Methods'
Prioritise — classically by Risk Priority Number, RPN = S × O × D (range 1–1000)
'Risk Prioritization number' — the correct term is Risk Priority Number

ul: Weakness of RPN: very different risks can give the same number — S = 10, O = 2, D = 5 and S = 2, O = 5, D = 10 both give 100 — and only 120 distinct RPN values exist among the 1,000 combinations.

Current alternatives: IEC 60812:2018 adds alternative RPN calculations and a criticality-matrix method. The AIAG-VDA FMEA Handbook (2019), used mainly in the automotive industry, replaces RPN with an Action Priority rating (High / Medium / Low), because equal RPNs can hide very different severities.
An earlier note on FMEA and RPN is at Simon Notes Part 3 · Note 21 (FMEA); treat any single RPN 'action threshold' as a company choice, not a standard.

sections.head: 🌳 Fault Tree Analysis (PDF 683)

body.p: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) identifies the combinations of events that lead to a specific failure. It is top-down and deductive: start from the undesired top event, break it into contributing causes, and use logic gates to show how they combine, down to basic events.

body.ascii:
TOP EVENT (incident)
                     │
                 [ AND ]
               ┌─────┴─────┐
         Primary cause   Primary cause
               │             │
            [ OR ]        [ OR ]
            ┌──┴──┐       ┌──┴──┐
         Event  Event  Event  Event   (basic events)

ul: AND gate: the output occurs only if all inputs occur — probabilities multiply (assuming independence).
OR gate: the output occurs if any one input occurs — probabilities approximately add when they are small (assuming independence).

Illustrative arithmetic: if each basic event has a probability of 0.01 per year, each OR gate gives about 0.02, and the AND gate gives about 0.02 × 0.02 = 0.0004 per year for the top event. Redundancy (AND) is what makes a top event rare.

FTA is used both before an accident (risk analysis, e.g. in FSA step 2) and after one (to test which combination of failures actually occurred). Its forward-looking partner is the event tree, which follows an initiating event through the success or failure of each safeguard.

sections.head: 🧀 The Swiss Cheese Model — Active Failures and Latent Conditions (PDF 685)

body.p: James Reason's Swiss cheese model is an accident causation model. Each slice is a layer of defence — design, procedures, supervision, training, alarms, the people at the sharp end. Every layer has holes, and the holes keep opening, closing and moving. An accident happens when holes in successive layers momentarily line up and let a hazard pass straight through all of them — the arrow in the source's printed figure.

Latent conditions
rows: What they are
Unsafe acts — slips, lapses, mistakes and procedural violations — by people in direct contact with the system (the front-line crew)
'Resident pathogens' built into the system by decisions of designers, builders, procedure writers and top management
When they act
Effects are felt almost immediately
Can lie dormant for years until they combine with active failures
How they work
Open short-lived holes in the defences
Create error-provoking conditions (time pressure, under-manning, poor equipment, fatigue, inexperience) and long-lasting holes (unworkable procedures, design or construction deficiencies)
Examples

A manufacturing defect (the source's example); inadequate manning; an unworkable SMS procedure; deferred maintenance; a design that hides a hot surface

ul: Why it matters: blaming the person at the sharp end closes one hole for one day. Finding and fixing the latent conditions closes holes for everyone — which is what ISM element 9 corrective action should aim at.
The model is one of several accident causation models; IMO does not prescribe it, but A.1075(28)'s systemic perspective — interactions between man, machine and organisation — is the same idea.
This is the bridge to the human-error questions in the source's exam insert: '80% human error' usually means active failures at the end of a chain of latent conditions (Part 27 · Topic 1).

ce_tip.text: When Senthil asks 'How do you do a root cause analysis?', start from ISM element 9 — corrective action must prevent recurrence — then show method: gather facts and the sequence of events; brainstorm causes with a fishbone; follow the strongest branch with 5 Why; test combinations with a fault tree if the event is serious; look for latent conditions, not just the active failure, using the Swiss cheese model; and close with corrective action aimed at the root cause. Add that IMO prescribes no particular tool — A.1075(28) calls them 'tools in a tool box'. Three slips cost marks: calling FMEA an RCA tool without saying it is proactive, 'Risk Prioritization Number', and defining a root cause as something that 'may or may not' cause the event.

qa: What is the difference between a proximate cause, a root cause and a contributing factor?

The proximate or direct cause is the event or condition immediately before the incident that directly produced it; removing it would have prevented the incident for the moment. The root cause is the underlying, often organisational, cause that set off the chain leading to the proximate cause; if it had been eliminated or modified, the whole chain and the outcome would have been prevented, and there are usually several. A contributing factor is something that may have contributed but whose removal alone would not have prevented the outcome. These are the NASA NPR 8621.1D definitions. In an investigation, proximate cause means the immediate cause; it is different from the insurance doctrine of causa proxima, which is the dominant effective cause of a loss.
Draw and explain a fishbone diagram for a purifier that keeps losing its water seal.

The effect, 'purifier loses water seal', goes at the head of the fish. The main bones are the categories — Man, Machine, Material and Method, and Measurement and Environment if using 6M. Under Man: wrong gravity disc selected, poor start-up sequence. Under Machine: worn bowl seals, operating-water valve leaking, low bowl speed. Under Material: fuel density higher than the disc allows, high water content. Under Method: no procedure for changing disc after bunkering a new fuel. Each cause can have sub-causes. The diagram lists possible causes; I then check each against evidence and use 5 Why on the ones that are confirmed. The example is illustrative.
What is Pareto analysis, and how would you use it as Chief Engineer?

It is the 80/20 rule: roughly 80 per cent of effects come from about 20 per cent of causes, a heuristic named by Juran after Vilfredo Pareto. I list a defined set of problems — for example a year of unplanned stoppages — sort the causes in descending order of impact, preferably downtime hours rather than count, plot them as bars with a cumulative percentage line on a zero-to-100 per cent scale, and act first on the few causes that make up most of the total. Pareto tells me where to look; fishbone and 5 Why then find the root causes. It makes my corrective-action plan under ISM element 9 evidence-based.
What is FMEA, and what is the Risk Priority Number? Is FMEA a root cause analysis tool?

FMEA, failure mode and effects analysis, is a systematic way of identifying how a system could fail, the effects and causes of each failure mode, and the controls in place, so that failures are prevented before they happen. Each failure mode is rated for Severity, Occurrence and Detection on 1 to 10 scales, and the Risk Priority Number is S times O times D, from 1 to 1,000. Because it works before failures occur it is a proactive risk-analysis technique rather than root cause analysis of an event that has happened, though the two complement each other. RPN has weaknesses — different combinations give the same number — so IEC 60812:2018 adds alternatives and the AIAG-VDA handbook of 2019 uses Action Priority instead.
Explain the Swiss cheese model, with marine examples of active failures and latent conditions.

James Reason's model shows an organisation's defences as slices of cheese, each with holes that open, close and move. An accident happens when holes in all the layers line up and a hazard passes through. Active failures are unsafe acts by front-line people — slips, lapses, mistakes and violations — with immediate effect: an oiler working without required PPE, an engineer opening the wrong valve. Latent conditions are built into the system by designers, managers and procedure writers and can lie dormant for years: under-manning, an unworkable procedure, deferred maintenance, a manufacturing defect. The lesson is that fixing latent conditions protects against many future errors, so corrective action should aim there rather than at blaming the individual.
Does IMO prescribe a method for root cause analysis in casualty investigation?

No. The Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), whose Parts I and II are mandatory under SOLAS XI-1/6, requires marine safety investigations but not a particular method. Resolution A.1075(28) of 2013 says analysis methods should be seen as tools in a tool box, chosen to suit the casualty. It requires a systemic perspective that looks beyond who did what to the conditions behind events, and the methods must at least support reconstruction of the sequence of events, identification of contributing factors at all appropriate levels, and safety analysis with recommendations. On board, ISM element 9 requires analysis and corrective action to prevent recurrence, and the company's SMS chooses the tools.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — An Auxiliary Engine Fuel Spray Fire (illustrative)
blocks: At sea, a fuel spray from a cracked low-pressure fuel pipe on a diesel generator ignites on an exposed exhaust section. The duty engineer stops the engine and the fire is put out with a portable extinguisher; there are no injuries. The company requires an investigation and corrective action under the SMS. The event and all details are invented for teaching.

Proximate cause: fuel spraying on to a hot surface. 5 Why: the pipe cracked because it vibrated; it vibrated because a support clamp was missing; the clamp was missing because it was not refitted after an overhaul; it was not refitted because the overhaul job card had no reassembly checklist; there was no checklist because the PMS job card had never been reviewed after the engine maker's service letter. Fishbone: Man (fatigue after a long port stay), Machine (insulation lagging removed and not replaced), Method (no reassembly check), Material (pipe of the wrong schedule fitted earlier). Swiss cheese: the active failure was not refitting the clamp; the latent conditions were the job card, the missing lagging, the workload and the unreviewed service letter. Pareto across the fleet shows that missing clamps and lagging cause most hot-surface reports, so the company acts fleet-wide. FTA confirms that the fire needed both a leak (OR: crack, loose joint) AND an exposed hot surface (OR: lagging removed, lagging damaged).

Corrective action targets the root causes: job cards revised with a reassembly checklist, lagging and screening restored and added to the PMS, service letters tracked. Preventive action uses an FMEA on the fuel systems of the other generators to find similar failure modes before they occur.

The examiner wants to hear the chain from the immediate cause to the organisational cause, the right tool for each step, and corrective action that closes latent holes, not just a reprimand. Saying 'human error — crew retrained' would fail this answer.

topics.definition: Under STCW regulation I/1 the chief engineer officer is the senior engineer officer responsible for the mechanical propulsion and the operation and maintenance of the mechanical and electrical installations of the ship. He must hold a certificate of competency as chief engineer under regulation III/2 (main propulsion machinery of 3,000 kW or more) or III/3 (750 kW to less than 3,000 kW). Indian candidates are expected to know how their own certificates are governed — the MS (STCW) Rules 2014 and TEAP — and that DG Shipping is now DGMA under the Merchant Shipping Act 2025.
A C/E may teach or assess at a maritime training institute later in his career; VICT and AECS are the gateway courses.
VGM, ESG and MACN appear as short-note questions; each is worth a crisp, correct definition rather than a long answer.

sections.head: 📦 Compliance Notes — VGM, ESG and MACN (PDF 689–690)

body.p: VGM — Verified Gross Mass. The total gross mass of a packed container: cargo items, packages, pallets, dunnage and other packing and securing material, plus the container's tare mass. Under SOLAS VI/2, as amended by MSC.380(94) and in force since 1 July 2016, the shipper must provide the VGM in the shipping document in time for stowage planning, and a packed container without a VGM shall not be loaded. It is obtained by Method 1 (weighing the packed container) or Method 2 (weighing all contents and adding the tare mass, by a certified method), per MSC.1/Circ.1475. The purpose is safe stowage — stability, stack weights, lashing and handling — not stability alone. India implemented it through DGS M.S. Notice No. 04 of 2016 (11 May 2016), later supplemented by further notices. Full note: Simon Notes Part 7 · Note 11 (VGM).

ESG — Environmental, Social and Governance. ESG is a framework of non-financial factors used by investors, lenders and charterers to judge a company's environmental impact, its treatment of people and communities, and the quality of its governance — transparency, accountability and ethics. There is no single standard ESG taxonomy.

body.p: MACN — Maritime Anti-Corruption Network. A global business network, established in 2011, working to eliminate corruption in the maritime industry; its vision is a maritime industry free of corruption that enables fair trade to the benefit of society. Its members are companies, not countries — mainly vessel owners and operators, together with other maritime companies such as cargo owners and service providers. MACN states it has over 225 member companies across more than 45 countries (October 2026; the figure changes). In India, MACN's collective action has included a DG Shipping-supported MACN India roundtable in December 2025. qa: What are the duties of a Chief Engineer under STCW?

STCW regulation I/1 defines the chief engineer officer as the senior engineer officer responsible for the mechanical propulsion and the operation and maintenance of the ship's mechanical and electrical installations. He holds a C/E certificate under regulation III/2 for 3,000 kW or more, or III/3 for 750 to less than 3,000 kW. At management level, Table A-III/2 requires competences including 'Use leadership and managerial skills' — task and workload management, effective resource management and decision-making techniques — along with personnel management and training and oversight of standard operating procedures. Section A-VIII/2 makes him, with the master, determine the needs of the voyage and ensure adequate engineering watch arrangements, and he issues standing orders and special instructions that the relieving engineer must read when taking over the watch.
What is the difference between TEAP Part A and Part B?

TEAP, the Training, Examination and Assessment Programme under the Merchant Shipping (STCW for Seafarers) Rules 2014, sets out training, sea service, examination and assessment for each certificate. Part A, Revision 1 of May 2015, is the programme itself, chapter by chapter on STCW lines, including revalidation and upgradation of certificates. Part B, of 2019, holds the appendices — the detailed approved-course syllabi and related rules. It is not correct that Part A is for initial certificates and Part B for revalidation. The controlled copy is on the DGMA website, and the 2014 Rules continue under section 324(2) of the Merchant Shipping Act 2025.
What are VICT and AECS, and who must do them?

Both are Indian courses for people who train or assess seafarers. VICT, the Vertical Integration Course for Trainers, replaced the earlier Training for Trainers and Assessors course; it runs 60 hours over 10 days under DGS STCW 2010 Circular No. 26 of 2018 (DG Shipping, now DGMA), is mandatory for training-institute faculty and instructors, and rests on IMO Model Course 6.09. AECS, Assessment, Examination and Certification of Seafarers, follows IMO Model Course 3.12 and is for faculty involved in assessment and examination. In both cases the approved institute issues a course-completion certificate; the courses meet the instructor and assessor qualification standards of STCW regulation I/6 and Section A-I/6, which do not themselves issue certificates.
What is VGM, and who is responsible for it?

Verified gross mass is the total gross mass of a packed container — cargo, packages, pallets, dunnage and other packing and securing material, plus the container tare mass. SOLAS regulation VI/2, as amended by MSC.380(94) and in force since 1 July 2016, makes the shipper responsible for providing it in the shipping document in time for stowage planning, by Method 1, weighing the packed container, or Method 2, weighing all the contents and adding the tare mass using a certified method. A packed container without a VGM shall not be loaded. The aim is safe stowage — stability, stack loads, lashing and handling.
What is ESG, and where does MACN fit in?

ESG — environmental, social and governance — is a framework of non-financial factors used by investors, lenders and charterers to judge how a company affects the environment, how it treats people and how well it is governed. It is not a single set of standards. In shipping, E covers the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy and the EU ETS, S covers MLC 2006 and crew welfare, and G covers governance and business ethics. MACN, the Maritime Anti-Corruption Network founded in 2011, is a governance example: a network of member companies — mainly vessel owners and operators, with cargo owners and service providers — working to eliminate corruption. It reports over 225 member companies in more than 45 countries; its members are companies, not countries.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — A New Chief Engineer's First Week (illustrative)
blocks: An officer newly promoted to C/E joins a 9,000 kW container feeder. In his first week he must set up his engine department and the ship calls at a port where an official asks for cigarettes before signing the clearance. All details are invented for teaching.

Certificate and role: he holds a III/2 certificate, required above 3,000 kW. Voyage planning: with the master he checks fuel, lubricants, chemicals, spares and stores for the next rotation (A-VIII/2). Watch arrangements and standing orders: he reviews the watch composition, issues his standing orders and night orders, and briefs that every relieving engineer must read them. Leadership: he plans the workload around port calls, assigns tasks by experience, and sets a rule that any engineer can stop a job he thinks unsafe. Port demand: following the company's anti-corruption policy (the company is a MACN member), the master and C/E politely refuse, record the demand and report it to the company. Containers: the cargo plan uses the shippers' VGMs; the engine department's concern is the ballast and fuel distribution that the loading computer uses.

STCW duties, company governance and cargo rules meet in daily work. The candidate who can name the instrument behind each action — A-III/2, A-VIII/2, the company's MACN-based policy, SOLAS VI/2 — answers like a Chief Engineer.
